ta-l1d8q5-d1e97.summary: Transitional paragraph introducing creaturely simplicity in three articles: whether any creature is simple, whether the soul is simple (which has special difficulty), and whether the soul is wholly in every part of the body.

ta-l1d8q5-d1e109.summary: First argument that some creature is simple. Form, which is incidental to composition, consists of a simple and invariable essence, and form is a creature.
claims: Form consists in a simple and invariable essence.

ta-l1d8q5-d1e112.summary: Second argument. The intellect's resolution does not stop while it finds composition, whether the parts are really separable or not, since many things are separated by the intellect that are not separated in act (Boethius). What the resolution finally stops at is wholly simple, and common being is such.
claims: The terminus of intellectual resolution is wholly simple.
Common being is the last term of resolution.

ta-l1d8q5-d1e115.summary: Third argument. If every creature were composite, it would be composed of creatures, whose components would also be composite, and so on to infinity, which nature and intellect do not allow. Otherwise one reaches first simple components that are creatures.
claims: Composition must terminate in simple components.

ta-l1d8q5-d1e119.summary: Anticipates the reply that the first components are not simple because they carry the concrete relation of being from another. But what is extrinsic to a thing does not compose with it, and the agent is extrinsic, so being from an agent introduces no composition.
claims: What is extrinsic does not compose with a thing.

ta-l1d8q5-d1e122.summary: Sed contra from Boethius: in everything below the first, that which is (quod est) and that by which it is (quo est) differ. Every creature is below the first, so it is composed of being and that which is.
claims: In everything after the first, quod est and quo est differ.

ta-l1d8q5-d1e128.summary: Second sed contra. Every creature has finite being, and being not received in something is not finite but absolute. So every creature has being received in something, and thus at least two things: being and what receives it.
claims: Being is finite only as received in something.

ta-l1d8q5-d1e131.summary: Thomas's determination. Whatever proceeds from God in diversity of essence falls short of his simplicity, but falling short of simplicity need not mean falling into composition, as falling short of the highest goodness need not mean falling into evil. Creatures are of two kinds. Those with complete being in themselves, like humans, fall short of divine simplicity by falling into composition. Since only in God is being his quiddity, every creature, bodily or spiritual, has its quiddity or nature and its being, acquired from God, and so is composed of being (quo est) and that which is (quod est). Others have being not in themselves but only in another: prime matter, every form, the universal, since being belongs only to a particular subsisting in nature. These are not composite. If one says they are composed of their nature and the relations by which they are referred to God or to what they compose with, those relations are either not things, and so do not compose, or things, in which case they are related by themselves, since what is a relation per se is not related by another relation. So one must reach something not composite that still falls short of the first's simplicity, either by being divisible potentially or accidentally (prime matter, form, the universal), or by being able to compose with another, which divine simplicity does not allow.
claims: Falling short of divine simplicity does not always mean composition.
Creatures with complete being are composed of quiddity and esse received from God.
Incomplete creatures (prime matter, form, universals) are not composite, but fall short of simplicity by divisibility or composability.

ta-l1d8q5-d1e134.summary: Applies the determination to the objections. The first arguments concern creatures without complete being, which are not composed of parts; the two sed contra arguments concern creatures with complete being.
claims: The arguments for simplicity concern incomplete creatures; those for composition concern complete ones.

ta-l1d8q5-d1e146.summary: First argument that the soul is simple. The soul is the form of the body (the Philosopher), and form is neither matter nor composite.
claims: The soul is form, and form is neither matter nor composite.

ta-l1d8q5-d1e149.summary: Second argument. Every composite has being from its components. If the soul were composite, it would have its own being, never removed from it. But the union of soul and body yields the being of the human, so the human would have two beings, the soul's and the composite's, which is impossible, since one thing has one being.
claims: One thing has one being.

ta-l1d8q5-d1e152.summary: Third argument. Every composition that comes to a thing after its complete being is accidental to it. If the soul, composed of its own principles, had perfect being in itself, its composition with the body would be accidental, and soul and body would make only an accidental unity, so the human would be a being per accidens.
claims: Composition after complete being is accidental.

ta-l1d8q5-d1e156.summary: Sed contra from Boethius: no simple form can be a subject. The soul is the subject of powers, habits, and intelligible species, so it is not a simple form.
claims: No simple form can be a subject.

ta-l1d8q5-d1e162.summary: Second sed contra. A simple form does not have being per se, and what has being only in another cannot remain after it or be a mover, though it can be a principle of motion, since a mover is a being complete in itself; the form of fire is not a mover (Physics 8). The soul remains after the body and moves the body, so it is not a simple form.
claims: What has being only in another cannot survive it or be a mover.

ta-l1d8q5-d1e165.summary: Third sed contra. No simple form has in itself a principle of individuation, since every form is common of itself. If the soul were a simple form, it would be individuated only by the body, and once the body was removed there would remain one soul, the nature of soul itself, not many individual souls.
claims: Forms are of themselves common and are individuated by matter.

ta-l1d8q5-d1e168.summary: Thomas's determination, weighing two opinions. (1) Some hold that the soul is composed of matter and form, some even that soul, bodies, and spirits share the same matter. Thomas rejects this. A form becomes intelligible only by separation from matter and its appendages, and naturally intelligible substances therefore seem immaterial, as Avicenna says something is intellective by being free from matter. Prime matter stripped of form has no diversity, and accidents cannot diversify it before substantial form. The first form received perfects the whole of it, and this is corporeity, which matter never loses (the Commentator). So matter exists only in bodies, and the soul has matter only in an equivocal sense. (2) Others hold that the soul is composed of quo est and quod est. Quod est differs from matter: it is the supposit having being, while matter does not have being, the composite does. In matter–form composites, quo est can mean the partial form, the act of being, or the nature resulting from form and matter (humanity). Since being composite is not part of the concept of quiddity, there can be a simple quiddity not resulting from form and matter. Such a quiddity either is its being, and then it is God, wholly simple, or it has being acquired from another, as every created quiddity does. Not subsisting in matter, it would acquire being in itself, so the quiddity is the quod est and its being the quo est. Since what has something not from itself is possible with respect to it, such a quiddity has potency and act, the quiddity being possible and its being its act. Thus in angels and the soul there is composition of potency and act, of quo est and quod est. They are simple forms in that their quiddity is not composed of diverse parts, but they are composed of quiddity and being.
claims: The soul is not composed of matter and form; matter exists only in bodies, since corporeity is the first form of all matter.
Created separate substances, including the soul, are composed of potency and act, as quiddity and esse.
A simple quiddity that is its own being is God; any other receives being from another.

ta-l1d8q5-d1e171.summary: Reply to the first argument. The soul is not composed of parts of its quiddity, any more than any other form. But because it is an absolute form, not dependent on matter, by its likeness and nearness to God, it has being per se, which other bodily forms lack. So there is composition of being and quod est in the soul, not in other forms, since being belongs not to bodily forms absolutely but to the composite.
claims: The soul has being per se as an absolute form, unlike other bodily forms.
Composition of esse and quod est applies to the soul but not to material forms.

ta-l1d8q5-d1e174.summary: Reply to the second argument. The soul undoubtedly has perfect being in itself, though this being does not result from parts composing its quiddity. Union with the body does not produce another being. The soul's own being becomes the being of the composite, since the composite's being is just the being of the form. Other material forms, by their imperfection, do not exist by that being but are only principles of being.
claims: The soul's own esse becomes the esse of the composite human; there is one esse.
Material forms are only principles of being, not themselves existing by it.
concepts: soul's esse communicated to the body

ta-l1d8q5-d1e178.summary: Reply to the third argument, following from the second. The composition that comes to the soul after its complete being, in our mode of understanding, does not produce another being, which would be accidental, so it does not follow that the human is a being per accidens.
claims: The human is not a being per accidens, since union with the body adds no further esse.

ta-l1d8q5-d1e181.summary: Reply to the first sed contra. If Boethius means a subject of any accidents whatever, his claim is true of a form so simple that it is its own being, which is God, and neither soul nor angel has such simplicity. If he means a subject of accidents with firm natural being that are accidents of the individual, the claim holds even of a simple form whose quiddity has no parts. Some accidents have no true being but are intentions of natural things, such as the species in the soul. Some follow the individual's nature through the matter that individuates it, like white and black in a human, and the soul cannot be subject of these. Others have natural being but follow from the principles of the species, as properties of the species, and a simple form can be subject of these, being not its own being because of the possibility in its quiddity. The soul's powers are of this kind, as the point and unity also have their properties.
claims: The soul, though a simple form, can be the subject of proper accidents following its species, such as its powers.
Only a form that is its own being, God, cannot be a subject of any accident.

ta-l1d8q5-d1e184.summary: Reply to the second sed contra. Every form is some likeness of the first principle, pure act, and the more it approaches his likeness, the more of his perfections it shares. Among bodily forms the rational soul comes closest to God's likeness, so it shares his nobilities: understanding, being able to move, and having being per se. The sensitive soul shares less, the vegetative still less, and so on. Moving and having absolute being belong to the soul not as form but as likeness of God.
claims: The rational soul, as closest likeness of God among bodily forms, shares understanding, moving, and subsistence.
Subsistence and moving belong to the soul as likeness of God, not as form.

ta-l1d8q5-d1e187.summary: Reply to the third sed contra. The soul has nothing in itself by which it is individuated; those who denied that it is 'this something' meant this, not that it lacks absolute being per se. It is individuated only by the body. So the error of those who posit souls created first and embodied later is impossible, since souls are made many only by being infused into many bodies. But although the soul's individuation depends on the body in its beginning, it does not depend on it in its end, as if it ceased when bodies ceased. Every perfection is poured into matter according to its capacity, so the soul's nature is received in different bodies with different nobility and purity, and in each body has being limited according to the body's measure. This limited being, though acquired in the body, is not from the body or dependent on it. When bodies are removed, each soul keeps its limited being according to the dispositions it acquired as the perfection of that body. This is Avicenna's solution. As an illustration: water divided among vessels keeps no distinct shapes when the vessels are removed, as material forms do not keep being per se, but wax shaped by different instruments keeps its distinct shapes when they are removed, and so the soul keeps its individual and distinct being after the body's destruction.
claims: The soul is individuated by the body in its origin, so souls cannot pre-exist bodies.
Once individuated, the soul keeps its individual being after death, not depending on the body for it.
Each soul's being is limited according to the body it informed.

ta-l1d8q5-d1e199.summary: First argument that the soul is not wholly in every part of the body. Being a simple form, the soul's wholeness lies in its powers, and not all its powers are in every part.
claims: The soul's totality consists in its powers.

ta-l1d8q5-d1e202.summary: Second argument. An animal is a composite of soul and body. If the whole soul were in every part, every part would be an animal, as every part of fire is fire.
claims: If the whole soul were in every part, every part would be an animal.

ta-l1d8q5-d1e205.summary: Third argument. The soul gives life to the body. If the whole soul were in every part, every part would receive life immediately and the life of one part would not depend on another, which is false, since the life of the whole body depends on the heart.
claims: The life of the body depends on the heart.

ta-l1d8q5-d1e209.summary: Fourth argument. The body has distinct parts, so if the whole soul were in each, it would be wholly in many places at once, which seems to belong only to God.
claims: Being wholly in many places at once belongs only to God.

ta-l1d8q5-d1e212.summary: Sed contra. A substantial form is present to every part of matter, perfecting not only the whole but each part, and the soul is the substantial form of the animate body.
claims: A substantial form perfects every part of its matter.

ta-l1d8q5-d1e215.summary: Second sed contra. The soul senses an injury equally quickly in every part of the body, which would not be so unless it were present to every part.
claims: The soul feels injury equally quickly in every part.

ta-l1d8q5-d1e218.summary: Thomas's determination. Some held that the soul can be considered by its essence, in which case it is not in the whole body but in a part, the heart, vivifying the whole through vital spirits, or as a potential whole integrated of all its powers, in which case it is wholly in the whole body but not wholly in each part, the parts of the soul relating to the parts of the body as the whole soul to the whole body ('if the eye were an animal, sight would be its soul'). This position rested on two false images: of the soul in the body as in a place, as mere mover and not form, like a sailor in a ship; and of its simplicity as that of a point with indivisible position. Both are foolish. With Augustine, and Albert, Thomas holds that the soul by its essence is wholly in every part of the body, but not by the totality of its powers, by which it is wholly in the whole animal. No simple substance has a place except through its relation to a body, and the soul relates to the body as the form from which the whole and every part has being, like a substantial form. But not all parts share all its powers. Some, the intellective powers, cannot perfect anything bodily, and the others are not poured into every part, since the parts differ in harmony and mixture and nothing is received except according to the receiver's proportion; ear and eye receive different perfections, though each receives being. So as form and essence the soul is wholly in every part; as mover through its powers it is wholly in the whole and in different parts by different powers.
claims: The soul by its essence is wholly in every part of the body as its substantial form.
By the totality of its powers, the soul is wholly in the whole body and in different parts according to different powers.
The soul is not in the body as in a place, nor simple as a point.
concepts: tota in toto et tota in qualibet parte
soul as form, not merely mover

ta-l1d8q5-d1e221.summary: Reply to the first argument. When we say the whole soul is in every part of the body, 'whole' means the perfection of its nature, not a totality of parts, since 'whole' and 'perfect' are the same (the Philosopher).
claims: 'Whole soul' in every part means the soul's complete nature.

ta-l1d8q5-d1e224.summary: Reply to the second argument. The perfectible must be proportioned to its perfection. Though a simple form, the soul is manifold in power, since diverse powers arise from its essence, so the body proportioned to it must have distinct parts to receive those powers; hence the soul is the act of an organic body. Not every part of an animal has that distinction, so not every part is an animal. Less noble souls with little diversity of powers perfect a body almost uniform in whole and parts, so when it is divided, distinct souls actually arise in the parts, as in annelids and plants. Before division, however, each part is an animal only potentially, as a part of any continuum exists only potentially, and a part of fire is something actual only after division.
claims: The soul is the act of an organic body, whose distinct parts receive its diverse powers.
In lower animals and plants, division can actualize distinct souls; before division parts are animals only potentially.

ta-l1d8q5-d1e228.summary: Reply to the third argument. 'To live' in an animal is said in two ways. It is the very being of the living thing ('for living things, to live is to be'), and in this sense the soul immediately makes every part live, as its form. It is also the soul's operation, which it performs in the heart as mover, life carried by vital spirits, first to the heart and then to all other parts. That is why, when the heart is injured, the soul's operation fails in all parts, and so does the parts' being, which is preserved by the soul's operation.
claims: Life as esse is given immediately to every part by the soul as form; life as operation flows from the heart.
Injury to the heart destroys the soul's operation and thereby the parts' being.

ta-l1d8q5-d1e234.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. The soul is not in the body or its parts as in a place but as form in matter, so it does not follow that it is in many places.
claims: The soul is in the body as form in matter, not as in a place.
concepts: form in matter vs. in place

ta-l1d8q5-d1e244.summary: An expositio textus. (1) Lombard lists fear, joy, and sadness as signs of the soul's multiplicity, though the Philosopher calls them passions of the composite. Love, fear, and the like are either bodily passions, which belong to the composite and do not remain in the separated soul, or acts of intellectual apprehension and affection, which belong to the soul in itself and remain after separation; the Philosopher even places delight in God. (2) God creates 'without need' because other agents act for an end other than themselves, which they need to acquire, whereas God does all things for himself (Prov. 16:4). (3) God contains all things 'without habitus': habitus refers to what surrounds a body like clothing, in which the body is contained. In bodies what is within is contained by what it is in, but in spirits what is within contains, as the soul contains the body. God contains things, being within all without being enclosed, so things are not related to him as clothing to the clothed. (4) 'God, who is life, does not subsist from composites': in a substantial composite perfection belongs to the whole, not to the parts. God is perfect in being, since he is life, which has nothing mixed in that is not life, and so he cannot be composed of non-living parts. He is perfect in well-being in three respects: in power, since he is virtue itself, not composed of powerless parts; in beauty, since he is light, not composed of non-luminous parts as crystal is of diaphanous ones; and in subtlety of nature, since he is spirit essentially, his quiddity not composed of dissimilar elements as humanity is of soul and body. He is 'living throughout' because there is nothing in him but life.
claims: Passions exist either as bodily passions of the composite or as intellectual affections that remain in the separated soul.
God acts without need, since he acts for himself as end.
Spiritual beings contain what they are in, so God contains all things without being enclosed.
God, being life, power, light, and spirit itself, cannot be composed of parts lacking these.
concepts: divine perfection in esse and bene esse

ta-l1d8q5-Dd1e92.summary: The Prooemium of Question 5 introduces creaturely simplicity in three articles: whether any creature is simple, whether the soul is simple, and whether the soul is wholly in every part of the body.

ta-l1d8q5-Dd1e101.summary: Article 1 asks whether any creature is simple. Thomas holds that whatever proceeds from God in diversity of essence falls short of his simplicity, but not always by composition. Creatures with complete being are composed of quiddity and esse received from God (quod est and quo est). Incomplete creatures, such as prime matter, forms, and universals, are not composite but fall short of divine simplicity by being divisible or composable. Appeals to relations of dependence cannot introduce a regress of composition.
claims: Complete creatures are composed of quiddity and esse; incomplete ones are non-composite but not perfectly simple.

ta-l1d8q5-Dd1e138.summary: Article 2 asks whether the soul is simple. Thomas rejects universal hylomorphism. Intelligibility requires immateriality, and matter, whose first form is corporeity, exists only in bodies, so the soul has no matter. He affirms instead that the soul, like the angels, is composed of potency and act, of quiddity and received esse: it is simple in quiddity but composed of quiddity and being. As an absolute form near to God, the soul has being per se, which it communicates to the body as the one esse of the human, so the human is no being per accidens. It can be the subject of proper accidents such as its powers. It subsists and moves as a likeness of God, and it is individuated by the body in its origin, which excludes pre-existence, yet it keeps its individual being after death (Avicenna's wax analogy).
claims: The soul is not composed of matter and form but of quiddity and esse.
The soul's esse is the one esse of the human composite.
The soul is individuated by the body but keeps its individuation after death.

ta-l1d8q5-Dd1e191.summary: Article 3 asks whether the soul is wholly in every part of the body. Rejecting the view that the soul by its essence is in the heart and the images of the soul as a sailor in a ship or as a point, Thomas holds with Augustine and Albert that by its essence, as substantial form, the soul is wholly in every part. By the totality of its powers it is wholly in the whole and in different parts by different powers, according to their proportion. Life as esse is given immediately to every part; life as operation flows through the heart. The soul is in the body as form in matter, not as in a place.
claims: As form, the soul is wholly in every part of the body; as mover through its powers, it is in different parts by different powers.

ta-l1d8q5-Dd1e239.summary: The Expositio textus of the simplicity section of Distinction 8 distinguishes bodily passions from intellectual affections, which survive in the separated soul. It explains that God acts without need and contains all things without being enclosed, and it shows from God's perfection in being (life) and in well-being (power, light, spirit) that he cannot be composed of parts.
claims: Intellectual affections remain in the separated soul.
God, as life, power, light, and spirit itself, is not composed of parts.

ta-l1d8q5.summary: Quaestio 5 of Book I, Distinction 8 treats creaturely simplicity, in contrast with divine simplicity. Article 1 holds that complete creatures are composed of quiddity and received esse, while incomplete beings (prime matter, forms, universals) are not composite but fall short of simplicity. Article 2 rejects universal hylomorphism, holding that matter exists only in bodies, and holds that the soul, like the angels, is composed of potency and act as quiddity and esse. The soul subsists as an absolute form whose esse becomes the one esse of the human. It is subject of its proper powers and is individuated by the body without pre-existing it, keeping its individuality after death. Article 3 holds that the soul is wholly in every part of the body by its essence, as substantial form, and present in different parts by different powers. The Expositio treats the soul's passions and God's self-sufficient, non-composite perfection.
claims: Every complete creature is composed of quiddity and esse; only God is wholly simple.
The soul is not hylomorphic but is composed of essence and esse, and its esse is that of the whole human.
The soul is individuated by the body yet survives as an individual.
The soul is wholly in every part of the body as form.
